Rest of Today through Tuesday...

Zonal flow aloft with an embedded shortwave moving northeast from
NW Wyoming today. This pattern will bring widespread showers and a
few potentially strong storms to SE Montana, but mainly dry
conditions to the western half of the forecast area this
afternoon. As to the severe threat, its a short window this
afternoon, and not as good a set up as yesterday. However there is
still some good CAPE (~1500-2500j/kg) and decent shear (~40kts)
for the few hours this afternoon. Heavy rain, strong wind gusts,
and large hail are the main threats with any storms. The strong
wind threat really looks confined to the heavy precipitation
cores, but could reach 70 mph in those cores. 

The shortwave shifts east this evening diminishing convection over
the east. Another wave moves in from the west mid-evening and will
provide the impetus for additional showers/thunderstorms
overnight, spreading west to east through the night. Severe threat
looks minimal with this activity, but thunder could certainly
disrupt sleep tonight. 

Another break develops in the morning as the overnight shortwave
exits northeast. Another wave arrives Thursday afternoon in a
similar fashion to this afternoons, impacting mainly the eastern
half of the forecast area. While a few thunderstorms are expected
tomorrow, the threat of severe weather is near zero. Additional
energy arrives over the western and central portions of the
forecast area Thursday night, though there is still some
uncertainty in the models with strength, location and timing of
this period of precipitation. The current NBM is showing high
precipitation potential (>50%) for most of the area overnight
through Friday morning. 

With the pattern aloft becoming more and more southwesterly as a
deepening trof takes hold along the west coast of the United
States, waves of energy will continue to flow over the area Friday
afternoon/night and probably will persist into Saturday. This is
reflected in the forecast with continued widespread precipitation
chances (30-60%) going into the weekend. 

Monsoonal moisture will ride the increasingly southwesterly flow 
aloft into the area over the next several days, tapering off (but 
not completely going away) by late Saturday into Sunday. At the 
same time will continue to bring low level moisture into the area 
from the plains, with a strong surge Thursday into Thursday night.
The combination of moisture fetches will boost Precipitable water
values well above normal (3-4 standard deviations) Thursday into 
Friday. This has prompted an Excessive Rainfall Outlook Slight 
Risk to be issued by WPC for the eastern half of the forecast area
during this period, and a Marginal Risk this afternoon through 
Friday for most other locations. This risk equates to the 
potential to exceed flash flood guidance and produce flooding. At 
this time the 1-3 hour flash flood guidance for most of the area 
is between 1.5 and 3 inches due to the lack of precipitation over 
the past few weeks. So, not planning any flash flood watches at 
this time since the forecast precipitation in the 1 to 6 hour time
frames don't look to exceed flood guidance at this time. In fact 
WPC probabilities for exceeding 2 inches of precipitation today 
through Saturday morning peak around 30-40% over NE Custer into 
Northern Fallon counties with the majority of the area under 20%. 
However will continue to monitor the threat closely as each wave 
of precipitation impacts the area. Bottom line we are looking at a
period of beneficial rainfall over the next several days, and 
through heavy downpours are likely at times, the potential for 
flooding remains low (slight risk east of a Roundup to Billings to
Sheridan WY). 

Temperatures will be 5 to 10 degrees cooler this afternoon 
compared to Tuesday, mainly due to cloud cover and shower 
activity. However the shift to northerly winds is helping as well 
as the source air is from a cooler region. The cooling trend 
continues into the weekend with forecast highs in the 70s for most
locations through Saturday. 

For the late weekend into early next week the pattern aloft shows
a persistent trof along the west coast with southwesterly flow 
over our region. There is some westward sagging of the trof though
that allows weak ridging to push into the area. This will 
diminish the stronger precipitation chances to start the week as 
well as allowing temperatures to rebound back toward seasonal 
levels. this pattern still favors chances for precipitation, 
especially the afternoon and evening showers/thunderstorm variety.
It looks like the hot/dry/smokey pattern is gone through at least
the middle of next week. Chambers
